title: Quyền Lực Đích Thực (The Art of Power)
author: Thích Nhất Hạnh
summary:
*The Art of Power* (published in Vietnamese as *Quyền Lực Đích Thực*) is Thich Nhat Hanh's direct engagement with a subject he approaches from an unusual angle for a Buddhist teacher: power itself, and the widespread but — in his view — mistaken belief that power, wealth, fame, and sensual pleasure are what bring genuine freedom and happiness. Rather than rejecting the desire for power outright, Thich Nhat Hanh reframes it: wanting power, recognition, or prosperity isn't inherently wrong, but pursuing them in the way most people and institutions currently do — chasing "looks-real" power at the expense of what's actually real — tends to produce more suffering than freedom, both for the pursuer and for everyone around them.

The book opens by naming the four things most people chase in the belief that they lead to happiness — power, fame, wealth, and sensual pleasure — and argues that without the training of mindfulness, these become traps rather than paths to genuine freedom, because they're pursued compulsively, disconnected from what actually produces wellbeing. Thich Nhat Hanh draws a central distinction between what "looks real" (conventional markers of power and success) and what "is real" (genuine freedom, security, and happiness), arguing that most modern institutions, including businesses, are built almost entirely around the former.

He then introduces "true power" as something built from five sources he identifies within Buddhist teaching — commonly translated as faith/confidence, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and insight — arguing that these produce a durable, non-harming form of power because they don't depend on external validation, comparison to others, or domination, and can't be taken away by circumstance the way conventional power can. He devotes significant attention to mindfulness practice specifically as the entry point for accessing this kind of power in daily life, including in business and professional contexts, and offers concrete practices (mindful breathing, walking meditation, "the two promises," and others) for readers to build genuine presence and freedom into ordinary working life.

A recurring theme, consistent with Thich Nhat Hanh's broader body of work, is that individual transformation and collective/organizational transformation are inseparable — that a business or community built by people practicing true power (rather than compulsively chasing looks-real power) produces both more genuine success and less suffering, for the people inside it and for the wider world it touches. The book closes with practical guidance on cultivating mindful community even within demanding professional environments, and on using whatever power, position, or resources one already has as a vehicle for reducing suffering rather than accumulating more status.

sections.title: Quyền Lực Đích Thực (True Power — What Does Power Really Mean?)
sections.summary:
This opening chapter poses the book's central question directly: what does power actually mean, and why does virtually everyone want it? Thich Nhat Hanh observes that our society is built on a narrow concept of power — chiefly wealth, fame, status, and sensual pleasure — and that pursuing these without mindfulness tends to trap rather than free the pursuer.

He introduces the distinction between "looks-real" power (what appears to bring freedom and happiness on the surface) and "is-real" power or freedom (what actually does), arguing that most people and institutions have never been taught to tell the difference, and so chase the former indefinitely without ever arriving at genuine satisfaction.

The chapter closes by previewing the alternative the book will offer: five sources of true power, rooted in inner cultivation rather than external accumulation.
keyLessons: Most people chase power, fame, wealth, and pleasure believing these bring happiness, without examining whether they actually do.
"Looks-real" power (external markers) differs from "is-real" freedom (genuine, durable wellbeing).
True power, as the book will argue, comes from inner cultivation, not external accumulation.

sections.title: Nghệ Thuật Sử Dụng Quyền Lực (The Art of Using Power)
sections.summary:
This chapter turns to how power, once attained in any conventional sense, is actually used — arguing that even legitimately-earned power or position becomes harmful if wielded without mindfulness, while the same power can become genuinely beneficial when the holder has cultivated presence and compassion.

Thich Nhat Hanh gives examples relevant to leaders and business figures, showing how unmindful use of power and pressure (chasing profit, status, and control at the expense of wellbeing) damages both the wielder and those around them, and that leadership grounded in mindfulness produces very different — and ultimately more sustainable — outcomes.

The chapter closes by connecting this to the book's practical throughline: power itself is neutral; what matters is the inner state of the person using it.
keyLessons: Power itself is neutral; its effects depend on the inner state and mindfulness of the person wielding it.
Unmindful pursuit of profit, status, and control damages both leaders and the people around them.
Leadership grounded in mindfulness produces more sustainable outcomes than leadership grounded purely in ambition.

sections.title: Nghệ Thuật Chánh Niệm (The Art of Mindfulness)
sections.summary:
This chapter introduces mindfulness practice as the practical entry point for developing true power in daily life, including specific techniques such as mindful breathing and walking meditation that can be practiced even within a demanding professional schedule.

Thich Nhat Hanh emphasizes that mindfulness isn't a retreat from daily responsibilities but a way of inhabiting them more fully and effectively — a mindful worker or leader, he argues, is more clear-headed and less reactive than one caught in constant compulsive striving.

The chapter closes by connecting mindfulness practice directly to the five sources of true power introduced earlier, positioning it as the foundational practice that makes the others accessible.
keyLessons: Mindfulness is presented as fully compatible with — and beneficial to — demanding professional life, not a retreat from it.
Simple practices like mindful breathing and walking meditation can be integrated into an ordinary workday.
Mindfulness is the foundational practice underlying the book's other sources of true power.

sections.title: Đạt Được Những Gì Ta Thực Sự Mong Muốn (Getting What We Really Want)
sections.summary:
This chapter examines the gap between what people believe they want (status, wealth, recognition) and what they actually want underneath that (security, connection, peace), arguing that mindfulness practice reveals this gap and allows people to redirect their energy toward what will actually satisfy them.

Thich Nhat Hanh uses the metaphor of chasing external validation as an unwinnable race, since desire for more status or comparison never resolves on its own terms, and contrasts this with the durable satisfaction available through presence and genuine connection.

The chapter closes by linking this insight to daily decision-making — encouraging readers to check whether a given pursuit is actually serving their deeper want, or merely the surface-level craving.
keyLessons: What people consciously chase (status, wealth) often differs from what would actually satisfy them (security, connection, peace).
Chasing external validation and comparison is presented as an unwinnable, self-perpetuating race.
Mindfulness practice helps reveal this gap and redirect energy toward what genuinely satisfies.

sections.title: Bí Quyết Hạnh Phúc (The Secret of Happiness)
sections.summary:
This chapter addresses happiness directly, arguing it is not a future state contingent on achieving power or wealth, but a present-moment capacity that can be cultivated through mindfulness regardless of external circumstances.

Thich Nhat Hanh offers concrete practices for generating happiness in ordinary moments (mindful eating, mindful conversation, gratitude practices), and argues that businesses and organizations that support their people's genuine wellbeing, not just their output, ultimately perform better and cause less harm.

The chapter closes by connecting individual happiness practice to organizational culture — a workplace of individually unhappy people, he argues, cannot produce a genuinely healthy or sustainable organization.
keyLessons: Happiness is presented as a present-moment capacity cultivated through mindfulness, not a future reward for achievement.
Concrete daily practices (mindful eating, gratitude, presence) build this capacity incrementally.
Organizational health depends on the genuine wellbeing of individuals within it, not just their output.

sections.title: Tình Thương Không Biên Giới (Boundless Love)
sections.summary:
This chapter extends the book's themes into compassion and love without boundaries — the capacity to extend genuine goodwill beyond one's immediate circle of family, friends, and colleagues to a wider community, including those one might otherwise see as competitors or adversaries.

Thich Nhat Hanh connects this boundless love directly to true power, arguing that a leader or businessperson capable of genuine compassion toward competitors and critics, not just allies, operates from a more secure and less reactive position than one who sees the world purely in adversarial terms.

The chapter closes by tying boundless love back to the book's practical throughline: this isn't presented as pure altruism disconnected from self-interest, but as a source of genuine, durable inner security.
keyLessons: Extending genuine goodwill beyond one's immediate circle, including to competitors or critics, is framed as a source of security, not weakness.
Adversarial, purely competitive framing of business relationships is presented as reactive and less secure than compassion-grounded leadership.
Boundless love is connected to true power rather than treated as separate from practical self-interest.

sections.title: Chăm Sóc Những Yếu Tố Phi-Doanh-Thương (Taking Care of the Non-Business Elements)
sections.summary:
This chapter addresses the parts of a business or organization that aren't directly about output or profit — employee wellbeing, workplace culture, environmental impact, and community relationships — arguing these "non-business elements" are actually foundational to sustainable business success, not peripheral to it.

Thich Nhat Hanh gives practical guidance for building mindful, humane organizational practices, drawing on his broader body of work on engaged Buddhism and mindful community-building applied specifically to a professional context.

The chapter closes by arguing that neglecting these non-business elements ultimately undermines even the narrowly financial success a business is trying to achieve.
keyLessons: "Non-business" elements (culture, wellbeing, community, environmental impact) are foundational to sustainable success, not peripheral.
Practical, humane organizational practices are treated as a business necessity, not just an ethical add-on.
Neglecting these elements ultimately undermines even narrowly financial business goals.

sections.title: Thắp Sáng Tỉnh Thức Cộng Đồng (Lighting Up Community Awakening)
sections.summary:
The closing chapter widens the lens from the individual and the single organization to community and collective transformation, arguing that mindful individuals naturally form and strengthen mindful communities ("sanghas"), which in turn support the individuals within them.

Thich Nhat Hanh closes the book by connecting personal practice of true power back to collective wellbeing — the ultimate purpose of cultivating true power isn't personal advantage, but the reduction of suffering for oneself and for the wider community one is part of.

The book ends, along with its appendices of specific meditation practices, by reiterating its opening question — what does power really mean — now answered through the lens of mindfulness, compassion, and genuine, durable freedom rather than accumulation or domination.
keyLessons: Mindful individuals naturally form and are supported by mindful communities, not just isolated personal practice.
The ultimate purpose of true power, in this framework, is reducing suffering, not personal advantage.
Genuine, durable freedom — not accumulation or domination — is the book's final answer to "what does power mean."
Wanting power, recognition, or prosperity isn't inherently wrong — how you pursue and use them determines whether they bring freedom or suffering.
Distinguish "looks-real" power (external markers like status and wealth) from "is-real" freedom (genuine, durable wellbeing).
Power is neutral; its effects depend entirely on the mindfulness and inner state of the person wielding it.
Mindfulness practice (breathing, walking meditation, presence) is fully compatible with demanding professional life, not a retreat from it.
What people consciously chase often differs from what would actually satisfy them underneath — check the gap regularly.
Happiness is a present-moment capacity you can cultivate now, not a future reward contingent on achieving power or wealth.
Extending genuine goodwill even to competitors and critics is a source of security and true power, not weakness.
"Non-business" elements — culture, employee wellbeing, community, environmental impact — are foundational to sustainable success, not optional extras.
Individual transformation and community/organizational transformation are inseparable; mindful individuals build and are supported by mindful communities.

quotes.text: "Muốn có quyền lực, muốn được danh tiếng hay giàu sang không phải là điều xấu." ("Wanting power, fame, or wealth is not, in itself, a bad thing.") — Thích Nhất Hạnh
"Nếu giàu có và quyền thế mà không hạnh phúc thì giàu có và quyền thế để làm gì?" ("If wealth and power don't bring happiness, what are they for?") — Thích Nhất Hạnh

"Đây được xem là liều thuốc tinh thần cho doanh giới với thông điệp khá sâu sắc: Ngưng chạy theo quyền hành, tiền tài, danh vọng và sắc dục." ("This book is seen as a kind of medicine for the business world, with a profound message: stop chasing power, wealth, fame, and sensual pleasure.") — described in Nhịp Cầu Đầu Tư coverage of the book

"Ta có thể vẫn kiếm lợi nhuận mà không tàn hại, mà phát huy công bằng xã hội, đem lại hiểu biết và giảm thiểu khổ đau." ("We can still earn profit without causing harm — promoting social fairness, understanding, and reducing suffering.") — Thích Nhất Hạnh

whoThisIsFor: Business leaders, professionals, and general readers drawn to a mindfulness- and compassion-based reframing of power, success, and leadership.
whenToReadThis: When feeling burned out by status-chasing or competitive pressure at work, or when looking to integrate mindfulness practice into a demanding professional life.

authorBio.name: Thích Nhất Hạnh
authorBio.bio:
Thích Nhất Hạnh (1926–2022) was a Vietnamese Buddhist monk, teacher, poet, and peace activist widely regarded as one of the most influential Buddhist teachers of the modern era in the West, second in global recognition only to the Dalai Lama according to some assessments. He founded the Plum Village tradition and monastery in France, along with practice centers around the world, and was a pioneer of "engaged Buddhism," applying mindfulness practice directly to social, environmental, and political issues.

Exiled from Vietnam for decades due to his peace activism during the Vietnam War (he was nominated for the Nobel Peace Prize by Martin Luther King Jr.), he built an international teaching community and authored over 100 books, roughly 40 of them written in English, covering mindfulness, meditation, engaged social action, and — as in this book — the application of Buddhist principles to modern life domains including business and power.

He returned to Vietnam in his later years and continued teaching until his health declined; he passed away in 2022 at his root temple in Hue, Vietnam. His teaching continues through Plum Village communities and the extensive body of written and recorded material he left behind.

conceptsFrameworks.name: Looks-Real vs. Is-Real (Power/Freedom)
conceptsFrameworks.definition: Thich Nhat Hanh's central distinction between what merely appears to bring freedom and happiness (external markers of power, wealth, fame, and pleasure) and what actually does (genuine, durable inner freedom). Most institutions and individuals, in his framing, chase the former without recognizing the difference.
conceptsFrameworks.sourceSection: True Power — What Does Power Really Mean?

conceptsFrameworks.name: The Five Sources of True Power
conceptsFrameworks.definition: A set of inner qualities — commonly rendered in translation as faith/confidence, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and insight — that the book identifies as producing a durable, non-harming form of power, because they don't depend on external validation or comparison and can't be taken away by circumstance the way conventional power can.
conceptsFrameworks.sourceSection: True Power — What Does Power Really Mean?

conceptsFrameworks.name: Non-Business Elements
conceptsFrameworks.definition: Thich Nhat Hanh's term for the parts of organizational life not directly tied to output or profit — employee wellbeing, culture, community relationships, environmental impact — which he argues are foundational to sustainable success rather than peripheral concerns.
conceptsFrameworks.sourceSection: Taking Care of the Non-Business Elements

actionSteps: Once today, before an important task or decision, take three slow, deliberate breaths and notice whether you're acting from compulsive striving or from a clear, grounded intention.
Identify one pursuit in your current work or life (a promotion, a sale, a status marker) and honestly ask whether it's serving a deeper want (security, connection, peace) or only a surface craving.
Practice one short walking-meditation break during your workday this week — walking slowly and deliberately, attention on each step, without a phone.
Extend one small, genuine gesture of goodwill toward someone you currently see as a competitor, critic, or adversary, without expecting anything in return.

Review one "non-business element" of your own work (your team's culture, your own wellbeing, a community relationship) that you've been neglecting, and take one concrete step to attend to it this week.
reflectionQuestions: What is a marker of "looks-real" power or success you've been chasing, and does attaining it actually bring you the freedom you expect?
Where in your life is your outer pursuit (status, wealth, recognition) disconnected from what you suspect you actually want underneath?
Who in your professional life do you currently relate to in purely adversarial terms, and what would it look like to extend genuine goodwill to them instead?

points: The book's central claim — that "true power" grounded in mindfulness produces better business outcomes than conventional power-seeking — is a values-based and spiritual claim more than an empirically demonstrated business-performance one; it's persuasive as ethical guidance but not proven as a competitive strategy in the way a management-science book would attempt to show.

Because the book addresses power, wealth, and business at a fairly high level of spiritual and philosophical generality, it offers less concrete, step-by-step operational guidance (org design, decision frameworks, metrics) than a typical business-strategy book, which may leave some business readers wanting more practical specificity.

The framing of profit-seeking as compatible with reducing harm and increasing fairness is a genuinely held and consistently argued position in Thich Nhat Hanh's broader body of work, but it doesn't grapple deeply with situations where profit incentives and harm-reduction genuinely conflict, rather than align.

As with any translated spiritual text, some nuance in specific terms (the five sources of power, for instance) may shift somewhat between the original English *The Art of Power* and the Vietnamese *Quyền Lực Đích Thực* translation; a bilingual reader comparing both editions may notice minor phrasing differences.
criticalTake.contextNote: This book sits within Thich Nhat Hanh's broader, decades-long body of work on engaged Buddhism and mindfulness, and is best understood as an application of that consistent worldview to the specific domain of power and business, rather than a standalone business-strategy text.

sourceNotes: Identified via web search as the Vietnamese translation of *The Art of Power* by Thich Nhat Hanh (2007, translated by Chân Đạt); the eight-chapter structure and chapter titles were cross-checked against a bilingual Vietnamese-English PDF listing on Budsas and corroborated by additional Vietnamese book-review sources. The Vietnamese-language quotes were drawn directly from Vietnamese source pages describing/quoting the book, with English translations composed by the assistant for readability — a bilingual reader comparing against the original English *The Art of Power* text may notice some difference in exact phrasing from the original English edition.
